claim: Previous mathematical models of the somitogenesis clock that invoke the mechanism of delayed negative feedback predict that the oscillation period depends on the sum of delays inherent to negative-feedback loops and inhibitor half-lives.
source: Previous mathematical models of the somitogenesis clock that invoke the mechanism of delayed negative feedback predict that its oscillation period depends on the sum of delays inherent to negative-feedback loops and inhibitor half-lives.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Lewis, 2003; Monk, 2003; Ay et al., 2013; Hanisch et al., 2013) mentioned in the Introduction section.

claim: A mathematical model predicts that increasing the half-life of NICD can lead to elevated NICD levels and an increase in the oscillation period.
source: The model predicts that increasing the half-life of the positive regulator, Notch intracellular domain (NICD), can lead to elevated NICD levels and an increase in the oscillation period.
evidence: This claim is based on the mathematical model developed in the study, with numerical solutions shown in Figure 1D-H.

claim: Exposure to XAV939 increases levels of NICD in the chick PSM.
source: Strikingly, we observed that the level of cNICD protein was increased significantly in the presence of XAV939 (Figure 4D, lanes 5, 6; n = 7/9; Table 1) compared to the corresponding DMSO control pool where the resident cNICD had degraded substantially in the presence of cycloheximide.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 4D and quantified in Table 1, with statistical significance (p = 0.0280).

claim: Exposure to XAV939 prolongs the half-life of NICD in the chick PSM.
source: We observe elevated levels and a prolonged half-life of NICD.
evidence: This claim is supported by the half-life measurements shown in Figure 6A,B, where the half-life of cNICD in untreated control embryos is 11.87 (+/− 4.97) minutes.

claim: Reducing NICD production rescues the effects of XAV939 on clock gene oscillations.
source: Reducing NICD production rescues these effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that exposure to 1 nM LY411575 together with XAV939 rescues the delay in clock gene oscillations (Figure 8I; n = 6/15).

claim: Somites form with a periodicity of every 90 minutes in the chicken.
source: Mesodermal segments, or somites, 'pinch off' at the rostral limit of the two rods of pre-somitic mesoderm (PSM) that lie on either side of the caudal neural tube, with a distinct, species-specific periodicity; every 90 min in the chicken and every 120 min in the mouse.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction, with reference to the broader literature (reviewed in Oates et al., 2012).

claim: Somites form with a periodicity of every 120 minutes in the mouse.
source: Mesodermal segments, or somites, 'pinch off' at the rostral limit of the two rods of pre-somitic mesoderm (PSM) that lie on either side of the caudal neural tube, with a distinct, species-specific periodicity; every 90 min in the chicken and every 120 min in the mouse.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction, with reference to the broader literature (reviewed in Oates et al., 2012).

claim: Clock genes belong to the Notch, WNT and FGF signalling pathways.
source: These 'clock' genes belong to the Notch, WNT and FGF signalling pathways and are expressed in a cyclical pattern in the PSM of a wide variety of vertebrate species (Krol et al., 2011; reviewed in Dequéant et al., 2008; Gibb et al., 2010; Maroto et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Krol et al., 2011; reviewed in Dequéant et al., 2008; Gibb et al., 2010; Maroto et al., 2012).

claim: Oscillatory gene expression in the vertebrate PSM is believed to be established through negative feedback loops of unstable clock gene products.
source: On a single cell level in the vertebrate PSM, oscillatory gene expression is believed to be established through negative feedback loops of unstable clock gene products.
evidence: This is stated as a prevailing hypothesis in the field, based on the broader literature context.

claim: The clock period can be altered by genetically modifying genes that encode negative regulators such as Hes7, Her6, Her7, and Nrarp.
source: Subsequent studies have confirmed that the period can be altered by genetically modifying genes that encode negative regulators (e.g., Hes7, Her6, Her7, Nrarp) (Herrgen et al., 2010; Schröter and Oates, 2010; Kim et al., 2011; Takashima et al., 2011; Oates et al., 2012; Harima, et al., 2013; Hoyle and Ish-Horowicz, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies (Herrgen et al., 2010; Schröter and Oates, 2010; Kim et al., 2011; Takashima et al., 2011; Oates et al., 2012; Harima, et al., 2013; Hoyle and Ish-Horowicz, 2013).

claim: Regulation of clock gene mRNA turnover and degradation is gene specific and regulated at the level of the 3′UTR.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that regulation of clock gene mRNA turnover and degradation is gene specific and regulated at the level of the 3′UTR (Hilgers et al., 2005; Nitanda et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Hilgers et al., 2005; Nitanda et al., 2014).

claim: There has been relatively little experimental work demonstrating the predicted role of protein stability in regulating the periodicity of clock gene oscillations.
source: In contrast, there has been relatively little experimental work demonstrating the predicted role of protein stability in regulating the periodicity of clock gene oscillations (Hirata et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the state of the field, with only one citation (Hirata et al., 2004) provided as an example.

claim: In zebrafish, Notch plays a key role in the synchronisation of neighbouring oscillators but is not necessary for oscillations themselves.
source: Moreover, in zebrafish there is experimental evidence that Notch plays a key role in the synchronisation of neighbouring oscillators (Delaune et al., 2012) but that it is not necessary for oscillations themselves (Ozbudak and Lewis, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Delaune et al., 2012; Ozbudak and Lewis, 2008).

claim: Notch signalling in mouse and chick is thought to be essential for oscillations.
source: In contrast, Notch signalling in mouse and chick is thought to be essential for oscillations (Ferjentsik et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Ferjentsik et al., 2009).

claim: NICD is unstable.
source: NICD is unstable and, at least in mouse, its production appears as pulsatile, spatio-temporal waves that traverse the rostro-caudal axis of the PSM in the manner of a clock gene (Huppert et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Huppert et al., 2005).

claim: NICD production appears as pulsatile, spatio-temporal waves that traverse the rostro-caudal axis of the PSM in the manner of a clock gene in mouse.
source: NICD is unstable and, at least in mouse, its production appears as pulsatile, spatio-temporal waves that traverse the rostro-caudal axis of the PSM in the manner of a clock gene (Huppert et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Huppert et al., 2005).

claim: Pulsatile Notch1 protein expression is dependent on Notch signalling in the PSM of both chick and mouse.
source: Importantly, pulsatile Notch1 protein expression was recently shown to be dependent on Notch signalling in the PSM of both chick and mouse (Bone et al., 2014); this raises the possibility that, in mouse and chick at least, positive feedback, mediated by Notch and NICD, plays a role in the clock mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Bone et al., 2014).

claim: In the mathematical model, increasing the NICD half-life increases the period of the oscillation and the levels of both NICD and clock protein.
source: In Figure 1D we show that increasing the NICD half-life increases the period of the oscillation and the levels of both NICD and clock protein.
evidence: This claim is based on numerical solutions of the mathematical model shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In the mathematical model, increasing the clock protein half-life does not greatly affect the oscillator period but reduces levels of NICD.
source: In Figure 1E we show that increasing the clock protein half-life does not greatly affect the oscillator period but reduces levels of NICD.
evidence: This claim is based on numerical solutions of the mathematical model shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In the mathematical model, the oscillator period and levels of NICD increase with NICD half-life but these effects are not seen upon increasing the clock protein half-life.
source: In Figure 1F,G we show that the oscillator period and levels of NICD increase with NICD half-life but that these effects are not seen upon increasing the clock protein half-life.
evidence: This claim is based on numerical solutions of the mathematical model shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: In the mathematical model, the increased period arising from increased NICD half-life can be rescued by reducing the NICD production rate.
source: In Figure 1H we show that the increased period, arising as a consequence of increased NICD half-life, can be rescued by reducing the NICD production rate.
evidence: This claim is based on numerical solutions of the mathematical model shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Treatment with 100 μM XAV939 causes robust and reproducible down regulation of the Wnt target genes cAxin2 and cLef1 in chick PSM explants.
source: Following a titration assay, we determined that 100 μM XAV939 treatment was the lowest concentration that caused robust and reproducible down regulation of the Wnt target genes cAxin2 and cLef1 compared to the corresponding DMSO-treated contralateral explants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D; n = 61/68; Bone et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Treatment with 100 μM XAV939 leads to increased levels of phosphorylated β-catenin at Ser33, Ser37, Thr41 in chick PSM explants.
source: Using the same assay, we investigated the effect of the inhibitor on the dynamic expression of cLfng in the PSM. Following exposure to 100 μM XAV939, the domain of cLfng expression was at least 1 phase behind that of the control explant (Figure 2A, M; n = 57/64) and occasionally this resulted in the treated explant forming one less somite boundary than the control explant.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A (n = 8/10; mean fold change = 2.856, p = 0.016).

claim: Following exposure to 100 μM XAV939, the domain of cLfng expression is at least 1 phase behind that of the control explant in chick PSM.
source: Following exposure to 100 μM XAV939, the domain of cLfng expression was at least 1 phase behind that of the control explant (Figure 2A, M; n = 57/64) and occasionally this resulted in the treated explant forming one less somite boundary than the control explant.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A,M (n = 57/64).

claim: cLfng expression is still dynamic in the presence of 100 μM XAV939 in chick PSM.
source: In order to ensure that the oscillations were delayed and not halted, a fix and culture assay (see 'Materials and methods') revealed that cLfng expression was still dynamic in the presence of 100 μM XAV939 (Figure 2B; n = 8/9).
evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture assay data shown in Figure 2B (n = 8/9).

claim: Neither proliferation nor apoptosis are significantly affected by 100 μM XAV939 treatment in chick PSM.
source: Furthermore, Phospho-histone H3 (pH3) and NucView analyses demonstrated that neither proliferation nor apoptosis, respectively, were significantly affected following drug treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,D; n = 4, p = 0.236; n = 4, p = 0.292).
evidence: This claim is supported by pH3 and NucView analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,D (n = 4, p = 0.236; n = 4, p = 0.292).

claim: Wnt inhibition delays the period of the segmentation clock in the chick PSM.
source: These data clearly demonstrate that Wnt inhibition delays the period of the segmentation clock in the chick PSM.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing delayed cLfng expression following XAV939 treatment.

claim: Exposure to 100 μM XAV939 delays the pace of mLfng oscillations in mouse PSM explants.
source: Using the same half-embryo inhibitor assay in the mouse embryo, we found that exposure to 100 μM XAV939 delayed the pace of mLfng oscillations as compared to control DMSO-treated E10.5 half PSM explants (Figure 2I; n = 19/26).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2I (n = 19/26).

claim: mLfng expression is still dynamic in the presence of 100 μM XAV939 in mouse PSM.
source: Moreover, a fix and culture assay revealed that mLfng expression was still dynamic in the presence of 100 μM XAV939 (Figure 2J; n = 12/20).
evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture assay data shown in Figure 2J (n = 12/20).

claim: At 25 μM, Cyclopamine abolishes expression of the Shh target gene cGli1 in the chicken half-PSM explant.
source: At 25 μM, Cyclopamine abolished expression of the Shh target gene cGli1 in the chicken half-PSM explant compared to the DMSO control (Figure 3A; n = 5/5).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A (n = 5/5).

claim: cLfng expression in the PSM is not delayed by Cyclopamine at either 25 μM or 50 μM.
source: Surprisingly, and in contrast to published data (Resende et al., 2010), cLfng expression in the PSM was not delayed at either 25 μM (Figure 3B,D; n = 6/9) or 50 μM (Figure 3C,D; n = 3/4).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3B,C,D (n = 6/9 at 25 μM; n = 3/4 at 50 μM).

claim: Shh signalling does not play a direct role in the regulation of the segmentation clock.
source: This assay suggests that Shh signalling does not play a direct role in the regulation of the segmentation clock.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no effect of Cyclopamine on cLfng expression.

claim: NICD stability is known to be regulated by GSK3B in other contexts.
source: Given our results with the Wnt inhibitor and that NICD stability is known, in other contexts, to be regulated by GSK3B (Espinosa et al., 2003; Jin et al., 2009; see also Foltz et al., 2002), we investigated whether the effect upon the period was associated with a change in levels of NICD, as the model predicted.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Espinosa et al., 2003; Jin et al., 2009; see also Foltz et al., 2002).

claim: The anti-cNICD antibody detects a specific band against endogenous cNICD that runs at the same size as recombinant cNICD protein and at the predicted molecular weight of ∼87 kDa.
source: Western Blot revealed a specific band against endogenous cNICD that ran at the same size as recombinant cNICD protein and at the predicted molecular weight of ∼87 kDa in the DMSO control pool which was abolished in the +LY411575 treated pool, thereby validating the specificity of the antibody (Figure 4A, lanes 3, 4; Figure 4D, lanes 1, 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4D.

claim: cNICD exhibits a spatial localisation profile in the chick PSM that is very similar to that described for mNICD in the mouse PSM.
source: We performed immunohistochemistry on sagittal sections of chick PSM tissue to analyse the spatial localisation profile of NICD in this tissue and found it to exhibit a very similar profile to that described for mNICD in the mouse PSM (Huppert et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B and comparison to previous work (Huppert et al., 2005).

claim: cNICD is produced in (and cleared from) discrete domains of the PSM in a manner reminiscent of the expression profile of clock genes in different phases of the cycle.
source: Thus cNICD is produced in (and cleared from) discrete domains of the PSM in a manner reminiscent of the expression profile of clock genes in different phases of the cycle (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Exposure to XAV939 elevates the level of cNICD protein in the chicken PSM.
source: These assays reveal that exposure to XAV939 elevates the level of cNICD protein in the chicken PSM, just as it delays oscillations of the Notch target gene cLfng.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, with statistical significance.

claim: Exposure to Cyclopamine does not affect the levels of cNICD in treated PSM explants.
source: Significantly, exposure to Cyclopamine did not affect the levels of cNICD in treated PSM explants just as it did not affect the pace of cLfng oscillations in this tissue (Figure 4D, lanes 13, 14; n = 2/2; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 4D, lanes 13, 14 (n = 2/2; Table 1).

claim: Exposure to XAV939 increases the level of mNICD protein in the mouse PSM.
source: Strikingly, we observed that the level of mNICD protein in the PSM was increased significantly in the presence of XAV939 (Figure 4E, lanes 3, 4; n = 8) compared to the corresponding DMSO control pool of half PSM explants, where mNICD levels had dropped substantially in the presence of cycloheximide (Figure 4E, lanes 1, 2; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 4E (n = 8) and quantified in Table 1.

claim: The effect of XAV939 to delay the pace of Lfng oscillations across the PSM and to increase the level of NICD in the PSM is conserved in both chick and mouse.
source: Thus, the effect of XAV939 to delay the pace of Lfng oscillations across the PSM and to increase the level of NICD in the PSM is conserved in both chick and mouse.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing similar effects in both chick and mouse.

claim: The stability of NICD in other contexts can be regulated by cyclin dependent kinase (CDK) mediated phosphorylation.
source: Previous studies have shown that the stability of NICD in other contexts can be regulated by cyclin dependent kinase (CDK) mediated phosphorylation (Fryer et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Fryer et al., 2004).

claim: Roscovitine is a 2,6,9-substituted purine analogue that competes with ATP for the active binding site on CDKs.
source: Roscovitine is a 2,6,9-substituted purine analogue that competes with ATP for the active binding site on CDKs (MacCallum et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (MacCallum et al., 2005).

claim: Roscovitine treatment at 10 µM clearly delays oscillation of cLfng expression in chick PSM.
source: We found that Roscovitine treatment at 10 µM clearly delayed oscillation of cLfng expression relative to the DMSO control (Figure 2C; n = 59/62)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C (n = 59/62).

claim: cLfng expression is still oscillatory in the presence of 10 µM Roscovitine in chick PSM.
source: whilst the fix and culture assay confirmed that cLfng expression was still oscillatory (Figure 2D; n = 8/10).
evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture assay data shown in Figure 2D (n = 8/10).

claim: Neither proliferation nor apoptosis are significantly affected by 10 µM Roscovitine treatment in chick PSM.
source: Neither proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B; n = 5, p = 0.204) nor apoptosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E; n = 4, p = 0.886) were significantly affected in the PSM.
evidence: This claim is supported by pH3 and NucView analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,E (n = 5, p = 0.204; n = 4, p = 0.886).

claim: Exposure to 10 μM Roscovitine delays the pace of mLfng oscillations in mouse PSM explants.
source: Moreover, we found that exposure to 10 μM Roscovitine delayed the pace of mLfng oscillations as compared to control DMSO-treated E10.5 mouse half PSM explants (Figure 2K; n = 20/22).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2K (n = 20/22).

claim: mLfng expression is still dynamic in the presence of 10 μM Roscovitine in mouse PSM.
source: The fix and culture assay revealed that mLfng expression was still dynamic in the presence of 10 μM Roscovitine (Figure 2L; n = 8/10).
evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture assay data shown in Figure 2L (n = 8/10).

claim: Exposure to 10 μM DRB delays cLfng oscillation phase in chick PSM explants.
source: We found that exposure of chick half-PSM explants to 10 μM DRB delayed cLfng oscillation phase compared to the control explant (Figure 2E; n = 67/73)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2E (n = 67/73).

claim: cLfng expression is still oscillatory in the presence of 10 μM DRB in chick PSM.
source: and the fix and culture assay confirmed that cLfng expression was still oscillatory in the PSM at this concentration (Figure 2F; n = 15/18).
evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture assay data shown in Figure 2F (n = 15/18).

claim: 10 μM DRB treatment reduces phosphorylation of Serine 5 on the CTD of RNA pol II in chick PSM.
source: Western Blotting analysis confirmed that phosphorylation of Serine 5 on the CTD of RNA pol II was reduced by 10 μM DRB treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; n = 3/3; mean fold change = 0.709).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B (n = 3/3; mean fold change = 0.709).

claim: Neither proliferation nor apoptosis are significantly affected by 10 μM DRB treatment in chick PSM.
source: Neither proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C; n = 5, p = 0.884) nor apoptosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F; n = 3, p = 0.844) were significantly affected.
evidence: This claim is supported by pH3 and NucView analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,F (n = 5, p = 0.884; n = 3, p = 0.844).

claim: Exposure to 1 μM PHA-767491 reduces phosphorylation of Serine 5 on the CTD of RNA pol II in chick PSM.
source: Similarly, exposure to 1 μM PHA-767491 reduced phosphorylation of Serine 5 on the CTD of RNA pol II (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; n = 2; mean fold change = 0.709)
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B (n = 2; mean fold change = 0.709).

claim: Exposure to 1 μM PHA-767491 delays cLfng oscillation phase in chick PSM explants.
source: delayed cLfng oscillation phase compared to the control half-PSM (Figure 2G; n = 13)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2G (n = 13).

claim: cLfng expression is still oscillatory in the presence of 1 μM PHA-767491 in chick PSM.
source: and the fix and culture assay confirmed that cLfng expression was still oscillatory in the PSM at this concentration (Figure 2H; n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture assay data shown in Figure 2H (n = 6).

claim: cHairy2 expression is consistently delayed by treatment with XAV939, Roscovitine, DRB, or PHA-767491 in chick PSM.
source: Another cycling Notch target, cHairy2, was also consistently delayed compared to the respective DMSO control when treated with either XAV939 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A; n = 4/6), Roscovitine (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B; n = 6/7), DRB (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C; n = 5/6) or PHA-767491 (n = 8/8; Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-D.

claim: A panel of CDK inhibitors robustly delays Notch target clock gene oscillations in the PSM in a manner separable from the cell cycle.
source: These data demonstrate that a panel of CDK inhibitors robustly delays Notch target clock gene oscillations in the PSM in a similar way to that seen following Wnt inhibition and that these effects are separable from the cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing delayed clock gene oscillations without significant effects on proliferation or apoptosis.

claim: 100 μM XAV939, 10 μM Roscovitine, and 10 μM DRB robustly down-regulate transcription of cAxin2 in the caudal chicken PSM.
source: We found that 100 μM XAV939 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), 10 μM Roscovitine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; n = 31/41) and 10 μM DRB (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F; n = 29/42) robustly down-regulated transcription of cAxin2 in the caudal chicken PSM, compared to the DMSO control.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: The increased phosphorylation of β-catenin at Ser33, Ser37, Thr41 observed with XAV939 is not observed following exposure to 10 μM Roscovitine or 10 μM DRB.
source: However, the increased phosphorylation of β-catenin at Ser33, Ser37, Thr41 observed with XAV939, which serves as a readout of Wnt inhibition, was not observed following exposure to 10 μM Roscovitine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; n = 5/6) or 10 μM DRB (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; n = 4/4)
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The mechanism by which Roscovitine and DRB inhibit transcription of cAxin2 is not through the inhibition of canonical Wnt signalling.
source: suggesting that the mechanism by which these CDK inhibitors inhibit transcription of cAxin2 is not through the inhibition of canonical Wnt signalling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Roscovitine and DRB do not increase phosphorylated β-catenin levels.

claim: The level of cNICD protein is increased significantly in the presence of Roscovitine in chick PSM.
source: Remarkably, and in agreement with model predictions, we observed that the level of cNICD protein was again increased significantly in the presence of Roscovitine (Figure 4D, lanes 7, 8; n = 9/10)
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 4D (n = 9/10) and quantified in Table 1 (p = 0.002).

claim: The level of cNICD protein is increased significantly in the presence of DRB in chick PSM.
source: DRB (Figure 4D, lanes 9, 10; n = 6/8)
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 4D (n = 6/8) and quantified in Table 1 (p = 0.008).

claim: The level of cNICD protein is increased in the presence of PHA-767491 in chick PSM.
source: and PHA-767491 (Figure 4D, lanes 11, 12; n = 2/2) compared to the corresponding DMSO control pool (See Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 4D (n = 2/2) and quantified in Table 1.

claim: Roscovitine, DRB and PHA-767491 treatments all increase the level of cNICD protein in the chicken PSM, just as they all delay oscillations of the Notch target gene cLfng.
source: Thus, Roscovitine, DRB and PHA-767491 treatments all increase the level of cNICD protein in the chicken PSM, just as they all delay oscillations of the Notch target gene cLfng.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data showing both increased NICD levels and delayed cLfng oscillations.

claim: Increased levels of NICD are associated with an increase to the periodicity of clock gene oscillations.
source: Hence, taken together the data with the Wnt and CDK inhibitors fulfil the predictions of the model that increased levels of NICD will be associated with an increase to the periodicity of clock gene oscillations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data and model predictions.

claim: Untreated control pairs complete one full oscillation and make an extra somite in 90 min.
source: Untreated control pairs completed one full oscillation and made an extra somite in 90 min whereas exposure to the reagents resulted in an oscillation period of approximately 120 min (n = 8 for each inhibitor and for DMSO; Figure 2—figure supplement 3E-J).
evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture time course data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E-J (n = 8).

claim: Exposure to XAV939, Roscovitine, DRB, or PHA-767491 results in an oscillation period of approximately 120 min in chick PSM.
source: Untreated control pairs completed one full oscillation and made an extra somite in 90 min whereas exposure to the reagents resulted in an oscillation period of approximately 120 min (n = 8 for each inhibitor and for DMSO; Figure 2—figure supplement 3E-J).
evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture time course data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E-J (n = 8 for each inhibitor).

claim: A longer clock period will result in the formation of fewer, larger somites in a given time, assuming a constant wave-front speed.
source: A prediction of the clock and wave-front model of somitogenesis is that a longer clock period will result, assuming a constant wave-front speed, in the formation of fewer, larger somites in a given time.
evidence: This claim is based on the established clock and wave-front model of somitogenesis.

claim: Fewer somites form in the presence of Roscovitine, DRB, PHA-767491, or XAV939 compared to DMSO controls after 6 hr culture.
source: Hence we analysed somite number in drug-treated explants cultured for an extended period of 6 hr and found that fewer somites formed in the presence of Roscovitine (n = 9, mean number = 2.11), DRB (n = 9, mean number = 1.94), PHA-767491 (n = 10, mean number = 2.5) and XAV939 (n = 7, mean number = 3.14) compared to DMSO controls (n = 15, mean number = 4.25).
evidence: This claim is supported by somite counting data after 6 hr culture.

claim: Lfng expression is still dynamic after 6 hr culture in the presence of XAV939, Roscovitine, DRB, or PHA-767491.
source: Additionally, using the fix and culture assay to confirm that the clock is still operating under treatment conditions, we observed that Lfng expression is still dynamic after the 6 hr culture period (Figure 5D–H; n = 5/5 for each reagent and for DMSO).
evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture assay data shown in Figure 5D-H (n = 5/5 for each reagent).

claim: There is a significant stepwise increase in somite size along the anteroposterior axis in embryos cultured in the presence of XAV939, Roscovitine, PHA-767491 or DRB as compared to DMSO control treated embryos.
source: Moreover, once the somites from the determined region of the PSM had segmented we observed a significant stepwise increase in somite size along the anteroposterior axis in the embryos cultured in the presence of XAV939, Roscovitine, PHA-767491 or DRB as compared to DMSO control treated embryos (Figure 5A–C,I–R).
evidence: This claim is supported by somite size measurements shown in Figure 5A-C,I-R, with statistical significance (p < 0.005 for all inhibitors).

claim: XAV939, Roscovitine, PHA-767491 and DRB treatments all result in an extension of the clock period and the formation of fewer, larger somites.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that XAV939, Roscovitine, PHA-767491 and DRB treatments all result in an extension of the clock period and the formation of fewer, larger somites.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data on clock period and somite formation.

claim: The higher levels of cNICD observed following exposure to XAV939, Roscovitine, or DRB is not due to increased production of NICD.
source: These data demonstrate that the higher levels of cNICD observed following exposure to the inhibitors is not due to increased production of NICD.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data showing elevated NICD levels even when new NICD production is blocked with LY411575 (Figure 4F).

claim: The half-life of cNICD in untreated control embryos is 11.87 (+/− 4.97) minutes.
source: From these data we infer the NICD half-life and find that it takes the value 11.87 (+/− 4.97) minutes in untreated control embryos (Figure 6A; n = 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by half-life measurements shown in Figure 6A (n = 5).

claim: In DRB treated explants, the half-life of cNICD protein is 29.59 (+/− 9.29) minutes.
source: Strikingly, in the DRB, Roscovitine and PHA-767491 treated explants, the half-life of cNICD protein is 29.59 (+/− 9.29), 22.01 (+/− 7.04) min, and 36.41 (+/− 8.88) min, respectively (Figure 6A,B; n = 4 for each inhibitor).
evidence: This claim is supported by half-life measurements shown in Figure 6A,B (n = 4).

claim: In Roscovitine treated explants, the half-life of cNICD protein is 22.01 (+/− 7.04) minutes.
source: Strikingly, in the DRB, Roscovitine and PHA-767491 treated explants, the half-life of cNICD protein is 29.59 (+/− 9.29), 22.01 (+/− 7.04) min, and 36.41 (+/− 8.88) min, respectively (Figure 6A,B; n = 4 for each inhibitor).
evidence: This claim is supported by half-life measurements shown in Figure 6A,B (n = 4).

claim: In PHA-767491 treated explants, the half-life of cNICD protein is 36.41 (+/− 8.88) minutes.
source: Strikingly, in the DRB, Roscovitine and PHA-767491 treated explants, the half-life of cNICD protein is 29.59 (+/− 9.29), 22.01 (+/− 7.04) min, and 36.41 (+/− 8.88) min, respectively (Figure 6A,B; n = 4 for each inhibitor).
evidence: This claim is supported by half-life measurements shown in Figure 6A,B (n = 4).

claim: DRB, Roscovitine and PHA-767491 treatments all significantly increase the half-life of cNICD protein in the chick PSM.
source: These data show that DRB, Roscovitine and PHA-767491 treatments all significantly increase the half-life of cNICD protein in the chick PSM.
evidence: This claim is supported by half-life measurements shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: An increased NICD half-life results in a longer clock period.
source: Thus, the data support the model prediction that an increased NICD half-life results in a longer clock period.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data and model predictions.

claim: NICD stability is known to be regulated by the Skp, Cullin, F-boxSel10/FBXW7 (SCF Sel10/FBXW7) E3 ubiquitin ligase complex.
source: NICD stability is known to be regulated by the Skp, Cullin, F-boxSel10/FBXW7 (SCF Sel10/FBXW7) E3 ubiquitin ligase complex (Gupta-Rossi et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Gupta-Rossi et al., 2001).

claim: MLN4924 inactivates SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes by suppressing neddylation of Cullin-1.
source: We tested whether turnover of NICD within the PSM affects the clock pace by repeating the half-embryo assay in the presence or absence of MLN4924 which inactivates SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes by suppressing neddylation of Cullin-1 (Soucy et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Soucy et al., 2009).

claim: Exposure of PSM explants to 1 μM MLN4924 leads to increased levels of phosphorylated β-catenin.
source: As a control, we analysed levels of phosphorylated β-catenin which is also targeted for ubiquitination and degradation by the SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase complex. As expected, exposure of PSM explants to 1 μM MLN4924 led to increased levels of phosphorylated β-catenin (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Exposure of PSM explants to 1 μM MLN4924 causes a delay in the pace of Lfng dynamic expression across the PSM.
source: Notably, exposure of PSM explants to 1 μM MLN4924 caused a delay in the pace of Lfng dynamic expression across the PSM (Figure 6C; n = 16)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6C (n = 16).

claim: Exposure of PSM explants to 1 μM MLN4924 increases levels of cNICD.
source: and increased levels of cNICD (Figure 6D; n = 3; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 6D (n = 3; Table 1).

claim: cLfng expression is still oscillatory in the presence of 1 μM MLN4924 in chick PSM.
source: The fix and culture assay confirmed that cLfng expression was still oscillatory in the PSM at this concentration (Figure 6C; n = 16).
evidence: This claim is supported by fix and culture assay data shown in Figure 6C (n = 16).

claim: Exposure to higher concentrations of MLN4924 (10–100 μM) results in progressively greater increases in the level of cNICD but abolishes dynamic Lfng expression across the PSM.
source: Exposure to higher concentrations of MLN4924 (10–100 μM) resulted in progressively greater increases in the level of cNICD but abolished dynamic Lfng expression across the PSM (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is stated but data is not shown.

claim: The mathematical model predicts that oscillations are only supported within a limited range of NICD (and Hes7) half-lives.
source: Notably, the mathematical model predicts that oscillations are only supported within a limited range of NICD (and Hes7) half-lives (See Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is based on the mathematical model results shown in Figure 1.

claim: A balance between positive and negative regulators is necessary for oscillations of the somitogenesis clock.
source: These data support the central thesis provided in this paper: a balance between positive and negative regulators is necessary for oscillations of the somitogenesis clock.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental and modeling data.

claim: 5 nM LY411575 significantly decreases cNICD levels compared to DMSO control in chick PSM.
source: In the presence of 5 nM LY411575, cNICD levels decreased significantly compared to the corresponding DMSO pool (Figure 7A, lanes 1, 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 7A, lanes 1, 2.

claim: In the presence of 1 nM or 0.1 nM LY411575, the levels of cNICD protein are similar to control DMSO treated contralateral PSMs.
source: while in the presence of 1 nM or 0.1 nM LY411575, the levels of cNICD protein were similar to control DMSO treated contralateral PSMs (Figure 7B, lanes 1, 2, Figure 7C, lanes 1, 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 7B,C, lanes 1, 2.

claim: The higher levels of NICD usually seen in the presence of Roscovitine alone are rescued by 1 nM LY411575 such that they resemble the levels of NICD in the corresponding DMSO pool.
source: The higher levels of NICD usually seen in the presence of Roscovitine alone (Figure 7D) are rescued by 1 nM LY411575 such that they resemble the levels of NICD in the corresponding DMSO pool (Figure 7B lanes 3, 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 7B, lanes 3, 4 and Figure 7D.

claim: The model predicts that reducing NICD production can rescue the effects of increased NICD half-life.
source: These findings concur with the predictions clearly proposed by our model (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is based on the mathematical model results shown in Figure 1H.

claim: 5 nM LY411575 severely reduces cLfng expression in the chick PSM.
source: 5 nM LY411575 severely reduced cLfng expression in the PSM (Figure 8A; n = 4/4)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8A (n = 4/4).

claim: cLfng appears largely unaffected in the presence of 1 nM or 0.1 nM LY411575 in chick PSM.
source: whereas cLfng appeared largely unaffected in the presence of 1 nM or 0.1 nM LY411575, compared to the control explant (Figure 8B,C; n = 22/25; n = 11/13, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8B,C (n = 22/25; n = 11/13).

claim: 1 nM LY411575 rescues the phase pattern delay caused by Roscovitine, DRB, or XAV939 in a significant number of explants.
source: Strikingly, we observed a rescue of the phase pattern in a significant number of explants cultured in the presence of Roscovitine, DRB or XAV939 together with 1 nM LY411575 (Figure 8G–I; n = 15/39, n = 8/20, n = 6/15, respectively)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8G-I (n = 15/39, n = 8/20, n = 6/15).

claim: 0.1 nM LY411575 does not rescue the delay caused by Roscovitine or XAV939.
source: Explants cultured in the presence of Roscovitine or XAV939 together with 0.1 nM LY411575 did not rescue the delay caused by these inhibitors (Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and data not shown; n = 0/9; n = 0/4).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 (n = 0/9; n = 0/4).

claim: Mathematical models that invoke delayed negative feedback have successfully explained numerous experimental observations of the somitogenesis clock.
source: Mathematical models that invoke the mechanism of delayed negative feedback have successfully explained numerous experimental observations of the somitogenesis clock (e.g., Lewis, 2003; Monk, 2003; Hirata et al., 2004, Ay et al., 2013; Hanisch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (e.g., Lewis, 2003; Monk, 2003; Hirata et al., 2004, Ay et al., 2013; Hanisch et al., 2013).

claim: The period of the somitogenesis clock can be approximated as a sum of the constituent delays and the half-lives of negative regulators.
source: An elegant prediction of the models is that the period of the somitogenesis clock can be approximated as a sum of the constituent delays and the half-lives of negative regulators.
evidence: This claim is based on previous mathematical models of the somitogenesis clock.

claim: Numerous studies have shown that genetic modification of clock components can modify the clock period.
source: However, whilst numerous studies have shown that genetic modification of clock components can modify the clock period, relatively little work has been published on whether half-lives of clock proteins have the predicted effect.
evidence: This claim is stated as an observation about the state of the field.

claim: In the mathematical model, NICD and the inhibitory clock protein compete to activate and repress the transcription of a clock gene, respectively.
source: In the model, NICD and the inhibitory clock protein compete to activate and repress the transcription of a clock gene, respectively.
evidence: This claim describes the structure of the mathematical model developed in the study.

claim: The release of NICD is a multi-cellular phenomenon involving the periodic and coordinated expression of cell surface proteins.
source: Notably, the release of NICD is a multi-cellular phenomenon involving the periodic and coordinated expression of cell surface proteins (Bone et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Bone et al., 2014).

claim: The predicted outcome of the model is that increasing the half-life of NICD elevates levels of NICD and lengthens the period of oscillations in addition to increasing levels of the inhibitory clock protein.
source: The predicted outcome of the model is that increasing the half-life of NICD elevates levels of NICD and lengthens the period of oscillations in addition to increasing levels of the inhibitory clock protein.
evidence: This claim is based on the mathematical model developed in the study.

claim: These effects can be rescued by decreasing the production rate of NICD.
source: These effects can be rescued by decreasing the production rate of NICD.
evidence: This claim is based on the mathematical model developed in the study.

claim: Treatment with small molecule inhibitors results in an increased half-life of the positive regulator NICD, which elevates the levels of NICD, delays the clock, and results in the formation of fewer larger somites.
source: When interpreted within the framework of the proposed model, these data support the hypothesis that treatment with the small molecule inhibitors results in an increased half-life of the positive regulator NICD, which elevates the levels of NICD, delays the clock, and results in the formation of fewer larger somites.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data and model predictions.

claim: The data do not support the hypothesis that the drug treatments solely modify the half-lives of negative regulators of the somitogenesis clock, such as Hes7.
source: In contrast, when interpreted within the framework of the proposed model, the data do not support the hypothesis, for instance: that the drug treatments solely modify the half-lives of negative regulators of the somitogenesis clock, such as Hes7.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data and model predictions.

claim: Both the delay in the pace of Lfng oscillations across the PSM and the elevated levels of NICD resulting from exposure to the small molecule treatments can be rescued by decreasing NICD production.
source: We also demonstrate experimentally, in agreement with model predictions, that both the delay in the pace of Lfng oscillations across the PSM and the elevated levels of the positive regulator, NICD, resulting from exposure to the small molecule treatments can be rescued by decreasing NICD production.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing rescue with LY411575.

claim: The effect of increasing the NICD half-life may be to alter tissue scale properties of the frequency gradient profile.
source: Nevertheless, it is also possible that the effect of increasing the NICD half-life is to alter tissue scale properties of the frequency gradient profile (e.g., increasing its rostro-caudal velocity or steepness would result in a greater proportion of cells in the PSM experiencing lower frequencies and thus observations of delayed phase patterns).
evidence: This is stated as a possibility based on inference.

claim: Positive as well as negative regulators of the somitogenesis clock can regulate its period.
source: Regardless of this detail, the premise of this study remains intact: positive as well as negative regulators of the somitogenesis clock can regulate its period.
evidence: This claim is the central thesis of the study, supported by the combined experimental and modeling data.

claim: The inclusion of both positive and negative feedback into the somitogenesis clock model introduces the possibility of interesting nonlinear phenomena that may have relevance to the somitogenesis clock.
source: We note that the inclusion of both positive and negative feedback into the somitogenesis clock model introduces the possibility of interesting nonlinear phenomena that may have relevance to the somitogenesis clock.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility based on the model structure.

claim: The inclusion of positive and negative feedback loops can result in the attainment of a wide frequency range over a small range in amplitudes.
source: For instance, Tsai et al. have shown that the inclusion of positive and negative feedback loops can result in the attainment of a wide frequency range over a small range in amplitudes (Tsai et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Tsai et al., 2008).

claim: A frequency gradient is thought to underlie the striking phase waves that traverse the rostro-caudal axis in somitogenesis.
source: This point is potentially relevant in the context of somitogenesis, where a frequency gradient is thought to underlie the striking phase waves that traverse the rostro-caudal axis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Inhibiting the Shh pathway does not affect clock pace or the level of cNICD in the chick PSM within the timeframe of the assay.
source: In this study, we clearly show that, in our hands, inhibiting the Shh pathway does not affect clock pace or the level of cNICD in the chick PSM within the timeframe of our assay.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with Cyclopamine.

claim: Wnt inhibition, elicited by exposure to XAV939, increases the half-life of NICD in the chick and mouse PSM, leading to elevated NICD levels and a prolonged period of clock gene oscillations and somite formation.
source: In contrast, we report Wnt inhibition, within a 3 hr time frame, elicited by exposure to XAV939, increases the half-life of NICD in the chick and mouse PSM, leading to elevated NICD levels and a clear and robust prolonged period of clock gene oscillations and somite formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined experimental data with XAV939.

claim: Gonzalez et al. previously reported exposure of mouse PSM explants to LiCl lengthens the period of Hes7 oscillations in the mouse PSM.
source: Intriguingly, Gonzalez et al. previously reported exposure of mouse PSM explants to LiCl, which acts to inhibit GSK3B, lengthens the period of Hes7 oscillations in the mouse PSM.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Gonzalez et al., 2013).

claim: The effect of LiCl on Hes7 oscillations may be via LiCl activation of the MapK pathway which is important for Hes expression in the PSM.
source: However, the authors report this effect may rather be via LiCl activation of the MapK pathway which is important for Hes expression in the PSM (Gonzalez et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Gonzalez et al., 2013).

claim: More specific approaches to elevate Wnt signalling have been shown not to change the endogenous period of the segmentation clock.
source: since more specific approaches to elevate Wnt signalling have been shown not to change the endogenous period of the segmentation clock (Aulehla et al., 2008; Gibb et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Aulehla et al., 2008; Gibb et al., 2009).

claim: Gonzalez et al. found the Wnt inhibitor CKI-7 delayed clock gene oscillations in the mouse PSM.
source: Moreover, Gonzalez et al. found the Wnt inhibitor CKI-7 delayed clock gene oscillations in the mouse PSM, in line with our own observations (Gibb et al., 2009; Gonzalez et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Gibb et al., 2009; Gonzalez et al., 2013).

claim: Three CDK inhibitors, Roscovitine, DRB and PHA-767491, increase the half-life of cNICD and delay the pace of Lfng oscillations at concentrations that have no significant effect on cell proliferation.
source: We demonstrate that three CDK inhibitors, Roscovitine, DRB and PHA-767491, also increase the half-life of cNICD and delay the pace of Lfng oscillations at concentrations that have no significant effect on cell proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined experimental data with CDK inhibitors.

claim: At higher concentrations of CDK inhibitors that affect proliferation, the oscillations of Lfng expression are abolished.
source: At higher concentrations of inhibitors that did affect proliferation, the oscillations of Lfng expression were abolished.
evidence: This claim is stated based on experimental observations.

claim: The effects of the CDK inhibitors on the segmentation clock are separable from those on the cell cycle.
source: Importantly, these data separate the effects of the inhibitors on the segmentation clock from those on the cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no significant effects on proliferation at concentrations that delay the clock.

claim: This finding is consistent with the 'clock and wavefront' model of somitogenesis, rather than a cell cycle based model.
source: This finding is consistent with the 'clock and wavefront' model of somitogenesis, rather than a cell cycle based model (Cooke and Zeeman, 1976; Stern et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citations to previous studies (Cooke and Zeeman, 1976; Stern et al., 1988).

claim: Tight control of the half-life of NICD, a positive regulator of oscillatory clock gene expression, appears key to regulating the clock period.
source: A striking finding is the fact that these very different pharmacological reagents share distinctive phenotypic outputs: increased levels and half-life of NICD and extended period of the clock gene oscillations. This raises the compelling prospect that these effects are causally linked.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data showing consistent effects across different inhibitors.

claim: Notch1 protein is dynamically and periodically expressed in the chick and mouse PSM in a Notch dependent fashion.
source: Recent data showing that Notch1 protein is dynamically and periodically expressed in the chick and mouse PSM in a Notch dependent fashion (Bone et al., 2014) demonstrate that Notch1/NICD is itself part of a positive feedback loop.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Bone et al., 2014).

claim: Notch1/NICD is itself part of a positive feedback loop.
source: Recent data showing that Notch1 protein is dynamically and periodically expressed in the chick and mouse PSM in a Notch dependent fashion (Bone et al., 2014) demonstrate that Notch1/NICD is itself part of a positive feedback loop.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Notch1 expression is Notch dependent.

claim: Under conditions where half-life of NICD is increased, the period of the clock is extended.
source: We experimentally validate the prediction that under conditions where half-life of NICD is increased, the period of the clock is extended.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined experimental data with various inhibitors.

claim: It is equally important to balance levels of both positive and negative input to correctly regulate the periodicity of clock gene oscillations.
source: Our data thus expand upon previous models by highlighting the necessity for an added level of regulation, namely the strict regulation of the half-life for the positive input signal, NICD. Hence, it appears equally important to balance levels of both positive and negative input to correctly regulate the periodicity of clock gene oscillations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental and modeling data.

claim: Nrarp-null mice display increased NICD levels in the PSM and a decrease in somite and vertebral body number.
source: This result is similar to observations made in Nrarp-null mice, which display increased NICD levels in the PSM and a decrease in somite and vertebral body number although the pace of clock gene oscillations and somite size was not assessed (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Kim et al., 2011).

claim: Extended NICD half-life is causally linked to the extended clock period.
source: Our data with the neddylation inhibitor MLN4924 further substantiate the hypothesis that extended NICD half-life is causally linked to the extended clock period, given that this reagent, which acts via a completely distinct molecular mechanism, nevertheless leads to the same phenotypic output as the Wnt and CDK inhibitors.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data with MLN4924.

claim: Exposure to MLN4924 elevates levels of phosphorylated β-catenin within PSM lysates.
source: In addition to elevating levels of NICD, exposure to MLN4924 elevates levels of phosphorylated β-catenin within PSM lysates.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western Blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In the absence of a degradation pathway, elevated levels of phosphorylated β catenin may continue to participate in target gene transcription.
source: However, we propose this is unlikely since in the absence of a degradation pathway the elevated levels of phosphorylated β catenin may in fact continue to participate in target gene transcription.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on inference.

claim: APC mutant lines which allow β catenin phosphorylation but are defective in ubiquitination are oncogenic, consistent with the idea that phosphorylated β catenin can activate target genes.
source: Indeed, APC mutant lines which allow β catenin phosphorylation but are defective in ubiquitination are oncogenic, consistent with the idea that phosphorylated β catenin can indeed activate target genes (Yang et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Yang et al., 2006).

claim: The extended period of the clock seen following exposure to MLN4924 is due to the elevated levels of NICD brought about via inhibition of NICD degradation.
source: Thus, we propose that the extended period of the clock seen following exposure to MLN4924 is due to the elevated levels of NICD brought about via inhibition of NICD degradation.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Overexpression or complete loss of Notch signalling abolishes clock gene oscillations and causes severe segmentation defects.
source: It has previously been shown that overexpression or complete loss of Notch signalling abolishes clock gene oscillations and causes severe segmentation defects (Niwa et al., 2007; Feller et al., 2008; Ferjentsik et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Niwa et al., 2007; Feller et al., 2008; Ferjentsik et al., 2009).

claim: There is a tolerance window for the degree of variance in levels of positive and negative input which will still allow for oscillatory gene expression.
source: These data, together with previous reports investigating the effect of modulating protein levels of key clock components (Hirata et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2011), indicate that there is a tolerance window for the degree of variance in levels of positive and negative input which will still allow for oscillatory gene expression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data and previous studies (Hirata et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2011).

claim: Slowing, as opposed to stopping, of the segmentation clock gene oscillations may be brought about through transient and/or partial stabilisation of Notch activity.
source: Taken together, our computational and experimental data show that slowing, as opposed to stopping, of the segmentation clock gene oscillations may be brought about through transient and/or partial stabilisation of Notch activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined computational and experimental data.

claim: In zebrafish embryos, the rate of tissue shortening, in addition to the periodicity of clock gene oscillations, is important in determining the periodicity of segmentation.
source: Finally, a recent report has beautifully demonstrated that in zebrafish embryos the rate of tissue shortening, in addition to the periodicity of clock gene oscillations, is important in determining the periodicity of segmentation (Soroldoni et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Soroldoni et al., 2014).

claim: The pace of the segmentation clock itself has a strong influence upon the pace of somite formation.
source: That analysis notwithstanding, our data nevertheless clearly show that the pace of the segmentation clock itself has a strong influence upon the pace of somite formation since significantly fewer somites are formed within a given time-frame when the pace of clock gene oscillations and NICD stability are affected.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing fewer somites formed when the clock is slowed.

claim: The stability and turnover of NICD is inextricably linked to the regulation of the pace of clock gene expression across the PSM.
source: In conclusion, our data suggest that the stability and turnover of NICD is inextricably linked to the regulation of the pace of clock gene expression across the PSM.
evidence: This claim is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from the combined experimental and modeling data.
